rv.q: These are among the best 90 minutes of theatre I have seen all year and the applause at the play’s end went on for so long that Collins began to look bashfully embarrassed.

Collins elevates a mediocre play into something that becomes properly affecting, thanks to a final scene which, after 80 minutes in which neither character has been fully themselves, achieves an undeniable degree of truth.
Running at just 100 minutes, the play takes too long to get us to care for these two characters.
The problem is that these face-offs have little emotional heft to them; rather, they feel aimless and worse yet, pointless.
Both actors have little to do other than present themselves and slightly inflect the first impression of flat-packed characters.
The good news is that it's only 90 minutes long; the bad news is that's still ample time to get fed up with it.
Really it’s just not good enough - everyone here has the capacity to make work better than Barcelona.
But on its own terms, it’s a thumping success.
It’s an odd construct but somehow it works.
Barcelona isn’t as weighty a piece as it sets out to be, but it is both funny and a little bit creepy.
Collins’s honest performance is both believable and relatable in this moment.

But overall, the production fails to rise above feeling contrived: it doesn't ring true that Manuel fails to ask Irene to leave as soon he tires of her and it also seems odd that Irene herself would run to the door, but not actually leave when things take on a more sinister tone.
It is funny, and if you want to sit back and enjoy a funny two-hander from a couple of charismatic actors, this play will do the job.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this two-hander, with some praising the performances and tight drama, while others dismiss it as flimsy star-vehicle fluff trading on Collins' Netflix fame. The 90-minute play sparks debate but often underwhelms.
